questions.q: What does OAuth 2.0 fundamentally accomplish, as distinct from SAML?
options: It proves who a user is, exactly like SAML
It authorizes access to a resource via tokens, without sharing a password
It only works for Salesforce-to-Salesforce integrations
It replaces the need for connected apps
questions.explain: OAuth is about authorizing access to resources through tokens. SAML, by contrast, is primarily about authenticating identity. OpenID Connect later layers identity on top of OAuth.

questions.q: Which OAuth flow is best suited for an unattended, nightly server-to-server job with no user present?
options: User-Agent (Implicit) flow
JWT Bearer flow
Device Flow
Username-Password flow
questions.explain: JWT Bearer uses a pre-registered certificate to authenticate the app itself, with no user interaction required and no refresh token to manage — ideal for unattended automation.

questions.q: Why is Salesforce retiring the Username-Password OAuth flow for connected apps?
options: Because it is too slow compared to other flows
Because it has never been supported in Salesforce
Because passing a raw username, password, and security token undermines modern protections like MFA
Because it only works with Salesforce Classic
questions.explain: Directly exchanging a username, password, and security token for a token bypasses much of what modern OAuth and MFA are designed to protect against, which is why Salesforce has scheduled its retirement for connected apps.

A specific permission that defines what a granted token can be used for
A synonym for 'profile'
The expiration date of a refresh token
questions.explain: A scope limits exactly what an access token's holder can request — for example, `api` for data access or `refresh_token` to allow renewing the token without the user present.

questions.q: Why should an integration that only reads Account records avoid requesting a 'full access' OAuth scope?
options: Full access scopes are not technically possible for Connected Apps
A leaked token is only as dangerous as the scope it carries, so narrower scopes limit the blast radius of a compromised token
Full access scopes expire faster than narrow ones
Salesforce blocks any app that requests more than one scope
questions.explain: Scoping tokens narrowly is a core security practice — if a narrowly-scoped token is ever leaked, the damage it can cause is limited to exactly what that scope permits.
